name: Earthjustice: healthy communities (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the air and drinking-water rules protect people in the United States.
summary: Earthjustice's healthy-communities work, toxics in air and water (our judgment: 25% of its programme spending, $34.3M in the year to June 2025): this model counts EPA's 2024 fine-particle (PM2.5) air standard, which Earthjustice's clients pressed for and defended in court (upheld in June 2026), and the 2024 PFAS drinking-water standards it defends, by EPA's own estimates of deaths avoided (up to 4,500 a year for PM2.5 from 2032; 9,600 over decades for PFAS), plus 50% for its other wins of fiscal 2022-2025 (chemical plants, coal ash, refineries, pesticides). At the defaults it comes to 0.015 years of healthy life per $1,000, nearly all from the PM2.5 standard; it is low because the deaths come years after the rules, advocacy is one cause of a rule and Earthjustice one of many groups behind it, and both rules' survival is in doubt. The biggest uncertainties are the years a won rule counts, the share of a rule due to advocacy and Earthjustice's share; both branches are discounted for missing data. Compliance costs to US water systems and industry aren't counted, as in the site's other policy models.

EPA's 2024 fine-particle (PM2.5) standard: premature deaths avoided a year once met (2032)

source.title: US EPA (2024), Final reconsideration of the PM NAAQS: overview fact sheet
source.quote: could result in as many as 4,500 avoided premature deaths and 290,000 avoided lost workdays in 2032

rows.explainer: EPA's estimate for 2032, the first year states must meet the stricter annual limit (9 micrograms per cubic metre, down from 12), against a baseline of the rules already in place. EPA's figure is the top of its range ('as many as'); the evidence row below takes that into account.

rows.label: EPA's 2024 PFAS drinking-water standards: deaths prevented over the analysis period

source.title: US EPA (2024), PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation: costs and benefits fact sheet
source.quote: Benefits will prevent over 9,600 deaths and reduce approximately 30,000 serious illnesses

rows.explainer: EPA's count of deaths the standards prevent once fully in place: 3,700 from heart disease, 2,000 from kidney cancer, 1,300 from developmental effects (birth weight) and 2,600 from bladder cancer, the last because treatment for PFAS also removes disinfection byproducts (counted as a side effect below).

rows.label: Of which: bladder-cancer deaths prevented because PFAS treatment also removes disinfection byproducts

source.title: US EPA (2024), PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation: costs and benefits fact sheet
source.quote: Bladder Cancer (resulting from co-removal of disinfection byproducts with PFAS) $380 million 2,600 deaths and 7,300 illnesses

rows.explainer: The part of EPA's deaths that comes from removing other contaminants along with the PFAS.

rows.label: Of which: deaths from developmental effects (low birth weight)

source.title: US EPA (2024), PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation: costs and benefits fact sheet

rows.explainer: Infant deaths from lower birth weight, valued below at the under-five value.

rows.label: Years EPA's PFAS benefit count runs over

source.title: US Government Accountability Office (2025), GAO-25-107897, on EPA's PFAS drinking-water rule
source.quote: annualized benefits over the 82-year analysis period

rows.explainer: EPA counts the benefits over an 82-year analysis period (GAO's account of the rule), so the yearly figure is the total over 82.

rows.label: PFAS standards: deaths from PFAS itself prevented a year, on average
rows.explainer: EPA's deaths less those from co-removed byproducts, averaged over the years counted. Deaths from cancer and heart disease come years after exposure falls, so the early years count fewer and later ones more; the average stands for both.

rows.label: Deaths a year the two rules avoid once in effect
rows.explainer: The two branches' deaths a year, for reading; each branch is valued on its own below.

rows.label: PM2.5 standard: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: Valued like every death on the site, by age band (GiveWell's moral weights, facts: moral_weights) × your value of a life. PM2.5 deaths in the US are mostly heart and lung deaths of older adults: the ages of cardiovascular deaths in a rich country (facts: death_ages, cvd_share_*_gbr, the UK, the nearest the facts hold to the US: 98% at 50 and over) stand in for them, not the world's air-pollution ages (which hold more child deaths).

rows.label: PFAS standards: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: By age band × your value of a life: the heart-disease and kidney-cancer deaths at the ages of US cancer deaths (facts: death_ages, cancer_share_*_usa), the 1,300 developmental deaths as infants (the under-five value). Deaths over 74 take the 50-74 value, the site's rule for want of an older band. The byproducts' bladder-cancer deaths (the side effect) are valued like the branch.

rows.label: Value of a death averted, average of the two rules (for reading only)
rows.explainer: The branches' own values apply; this is their average weighted by deaths a year, for reading only.

rows.label: Share of each rule due to advocacy at all (all groups together)
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for the part of a won US rule that is the advocates' doing rather than what the agency and events would have done anyway (facts: climate.advocacy_share_of_policy_win, 30%, 10% to 60%), stated for climate rules and taken here for EPA's health rules from the same agency and the same kind of petitions, comments and lawsuits. Earthjustice's part of the advocates' work is each branch's attribution row. The rules are in, so this is not a chance of winning.

rows.label: Years a won rule counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The shared number of years a won reform counts (docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: PM2.5 standard: years from the rule until its deaths are avoided
rows.explainer: States must meet the 2024 limit by 2032, EPA's analysis year, with cuts building from about 2028; designations, due in February 2026, were ordered by February 2027 and EPA is appealing. Our judgment, 8 years from 2024 (6 to 10).

rows.label: Discount for the wait
Years counted, discounted (before the wait)
PM2.5 standard: discounted years of impact
PFAS standards: years from the rule until its deaths are avoided
rows.explainer: Water systems must meet the PFOA and PFOS limits by 2029, which EPA proposes to push to 2031; the deaths fall as exposure falls after that. Our judgment, 6 years from 2024 (5 to 7).

rows.label: PFAS standards: discounted years of impact
PM2.5 standard: expected value before adjustments (units of value)
PFAS standards: expected value before adjustments (units of value)
PM2.5 standard: years lived with illness averted per death averted
rows.explainer: The shared figures (facts: death_ages): ambient air pollution's share of its burden that is illness (air_pollution_yld_share, 8%) over the deaths per DALY of cardiovascular disease in a rich country (cvd_deaths_per_daly_gbr, the UK standing for the US, as for the ages): each death averted comes with that much illness averted.

rows.label: PFAS standards: years lived with illness averted per death averted
rows.explainer: The shared figures for US cancer (facts: death_ages, cancer_yld_share_usa over cancer_deaths_per_daly_usa), standing for the heart-disease and cancer illness EPA counts.

rows.label: PM2.5 standard: illness averted before adjustments (DALYs)
PFAS standards: illness averted before adjustments (DALYs)
Expected value a year of the period, before adjustments (units of value)
Evidence adjustment: how far EPA's death estimates should be trusted
rows.explainer: EPA's PM2.5 figure is the top of its range (the larger of its two concentration-response studies; the other gives about half), and its PFAS deaths rest on dose-response models for heart disease and kidney cancer from observational studies. Our judgment, 0.7 (0.4 to 1.0), between face value and EPA's lower estimate; delivery and repeal are in each branch's implementation row.

rows.label: PM2.5 standard: share of the deaths that wouldn't have been avoided anyway
rows.explainer: EPA's estimate is already net of the rules in place; some of the cut would have come from coal closings and vehicle turnover beyond its baseline. Our judgment, 80% (60% to 100%).

rows.label: PM2.5 standard: Earthjustice's share of the advocacy resources behind it

source.title: Earthjustice (2026), Court upholds life-saving national soot air quality standard
source.quote: intervened to defend the strengthened soot standard

rows.explainer: Earthjustice was counsel to the health and environmental groups (the American Lung Association, NRDC, the Environmental Defense Fund and Sierra Club among its clients) that pressed EPA to tighten the standard and intervened to defend it in Kentucky v. EPA, which the D.C. Circuit upheld in June 2026 against industry, 25 states and EPA itself; Clean Air Task Force represented other intervenors, and states defended it too. Earthjustice then won an order that EPA designate the areas that fail the standard. Its clients' own work counts among the others' resources. Our judgment, 25% (10% to 45%).

rows.label: PM2.5 standard: share of the deaths actually avoided

source.title: Harvard Environmental and Energy Law Program, Regulatory Tracker: PM NAAQS
source.quote: On Nov. 24, 2025, EPA asked the D.C. Circuit to vacate the 2024 revision

rows.explainer: EPA asked the court to vacate its own standard in November 2025; the D.C. Circuit refused and upheld it (June 2026), states have petitioned the Supreme Court, and EPA missed the February 2026 designation deadline until a court ordered designations by February 2027. Meeting the standard also depends on state plans and on federal rules being rolled back. Our judgment, 60% (30% to 85%).

rows.label: PFAS standards: share of the deaths that wouldn't have been avoided anyway
rows.explainer: Several states (New Jersey, Michigan, Pennsylvania, New York and others) already had their own PFAS limits, some water systems were treating voluntarily, and PFOA and PFOS were phased out of US manufacture. Our judgment, 80% (50% to 100%).

rows.label: PFAS standards: Earthjustice's share of the advocacy resources behind them

source.title: Earthjustice (2025), EPA seeks to eliminate critical PFAS drinking water protections

rows.explainer: Earthjustice represents eight affected community groups (among them Clean Cape Fear and the Buxmont Coalition for Safe Water) defending the standards against the water utilities' and chemical industry's challenges and against EPA's own motion to vacate part of them, beside NRDC, the Environmental Working Group and many community groups that pressed for the rule for years. Our judgment, 15% (5% to 30%).

rows.label: PFAS standards: share of the deaths actually avoided
rows.explainer: EPA keeps the PFOA and PFOS limits (most of the heart-disease and kidney-cancer deaths) but proposes pushing compliance to 2031 and rescinding the limits for four other PFAS; the challenge in the D.C. Circuit is undecided. Our judgment, 60% (30% to 85%).

rows.label: Earthjustice's own spending as a share of its resources (with credit by share of resources)
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources on, the donated legal work and advertising space count as others' resources behind the same wins (templates.md Convention 2). Off (the default), 1.

rows.label: PM2.5 standard: share of credit used
PFAS standards: share of credit used
Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): no death averted is measured for Earthjustice's work; the deaths are EPA's estimates of whole rules and Earthjustice's part a judgment. Both branches take it.

rows.label: PM2.5 standard: all adjustments combined
PFAS standards: all adjustments combined
Share that wouldn't have happened anyway (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The branches' own rows apply; this is their weighted average, for reading only.

rows.explainer: The branches' own rows apply; this is their weighted average, for reading only.

Share of the wins delivered (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)

rows.explainer: The branches' own rows apply; this is their weighted average, for reading only.

rows.label: Side effect: bladder-cancer deaths averted by removing disinfection byproducts along with PFAS, as a share of the PFAS branch
rows.explainer: Treatment for PFAS also removes the byproducts of chlorinating water, which EPA counts as 2,600 bladder-cancer deaths prevented: a benefit beside the rule's own aim, 37% on top of the PFAS deaths.

rows.label: Other health wins of the period not modelled, as a share of the modelled value

source.title: Earthjustice, Annual Report, fiscal year 2025
source.quote: Collectively, these changes removed over 740 tons per year of toxic pollution from oil refineries in the region.

rows.explainer: The two rules are the period's largest countable health wins, but much of the work isn't in them: the 2024 chemical-plant and ethylene-oxide sterilizer rules, the 2024 mercury and air toxics update (since exempted for dozens of plants, which Earthjustice is suing over), coal-ash rules, the Fifth Circuit ruling that Texas and Louisiana must plan for interstate air pollution, the chlorpyrifos ban on food crops (2021, later vacated and partly restored), lead-pipe replacement, community enforcement cases (the Phillips 66 refineries near Los Angeles, over 740 tons a year of toxic pollution cut before they closed). Their spending is in the cost, so leaving them out would count them as worth nothing. Our judgment, 50% of the modelled value (20% to 100%): Clean Air Task Force's model takes 30% for a specialist's smaller set of other wins; Earthjustice's health docket is broader (several national rules a year besides community cases).

rows.label: All adjustments combined (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The branches' own combined adjustments apply; this is their weighted average, for reading only.

rows.label: Illness averted, credited, a year of the period (DALYs)
rows.formula: (pm_illness_downstream * pm_total_adj + pfas_illness_downstream * pfas_total_adj * (1 + pfas_dbp_share)) / period_years * (1 + unmodelled_benefits_adj)
rows.explainer: Each rule's illness × its own adjustments, spread over the period, with the co-removed byproducts' illness and the other wins as shares, like the deaths.

rows.label: Illness averted, in units of value
rows.explainer: The bridge from DALYs into units of value (docs/normalization.md 2.6): fixed, don't edit.

rows.label: Units of value a year of the period
rows.formula: (pm_downstream * pm_total_adj + pfas_downstream * pfas_total_adj * (1 + pfas_dbp_share)) / period_years * (1 + unmodelled_benefits_adj) + uov_from_daly
rows.explainer: Each rule's deaths × its own adjustments, summed and spread over the period's four years, with the co-removed byproducts' deaths and the other wins added as shares, plus the illness averted through the bridge.
